title: Как облажался сам Шеф  (How the Chef Himself Screwed Up)

segments.t: At the end of the shift, after Vika heads home, Lyova asks Chef Barinov how Max can survive such an embarrassing mistake. When Lyova asks if the great Viktor Petrovich has ever blundered like that himself, Barinov sighs and recalls the day he first laid eyes on Kristina before knowing she was Nagiyev's wife.
Как же ты живёшь с таким косяком?
Я уже от стыда повесился уже, наверное.
Now let's go back through the conversation line by line.
'Everyone has already gone home.' The plural past ending '-li' on the verb for 'we have gone' covers a group or the polite 'you'. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'I am heading out right now myself.' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'any minute', while 'am leaving' completes the thought.
'See you tomorrow.' In Russian, the idea of 'until' flows naturally into 'tomorrow' without extra filler words.
'And when are you going home?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'and' before landing on 'will go'. Lyova answers right away.
'I will work for a little while longer.' The grammar packs 'I' and 'to work for a while' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'You do not have a wife.' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'wife', while 'there is no' completes the thought.
'She would make a good wife.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'was' and finishing on 'wife'. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Как же ты живёшь с таким косяком?
'How do you even live with a blunder like that?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'how' and finishing on 'hers'.
Я уже от стыда повесился уже, наверное.
'I probably would have hanged myself from shame already.' Notice how Russian expresses 'I' and 'probably' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'You actually had that opportunity once.' Chef Viktor addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'possibility'. Lyova answers right away.
'Wait, when did I ever screw up?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'when' and finishing on 'screw up'.
'Let me remind you.' Chef Viktor brings out the contrast between 'will remind' and 'you' in a few short words.
'Now I am reminding you.' The grammar packs 'now' and 'reminds of' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Alright, let's hear the whole conversation once more from start to finish.
Как же ты живёшь с таким косяком?
Я уже от стыда повесился уже, наверное.
